accuracy.evidence: Checked against CCSS 4.OA.C.5 (its own example: rule 'add 3' from 1 alternates odd and even, explain why) and the NC England Y4-6 sequence statements. Every figure recomputed: 1, 4, 7 … 22; 100 = 1 + 33 × 3 so 100 is a term; 50 is not (49 is not a multiple of 3; terms go 46, 49, 52); 'add 4' from 2 gives 2, 6, 10 … 38 with last digits 2, 6, 0, 4, 8 repeating and no odd digit; matchstick row 3n + 1 (4, 7, 10, 13, 16; 10 squares 31, 6 squares 19); 4th term of 'add 5' from 2 is 17; 'add 10' from 3 always ends in 3; m2: 34 and 42 are 2 more than multiples of 4, 35 is odd.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets documented sequence slips (NCETM Y4-6 sequences guidance; Orton and Orton on pattern generalisation): multiplying when the rule says add (×3 chips in step 1), counting one jump too many for the nth term (22 for the 4th term), judging a feature from one or two terms, believing every rule alternates odd and even (add 2 test), assuming 'going up' means hitting a target number (50), and the n × 4 matchstick over-count of shared sides plus the 3n under-count. Each has its own lab or challenge message.

lab_distinct.evidence: gate_lab_distinct passed under the 30% shingle limit, including flag_linseq.js (term-to-term rule, 10th term), flag_twoseq.js (two rules side by side), flag_pat.js (repeating units) and flag_oddev.js. No other lab labels parity term by term, compares odd and even step sizes with paired dot pictures, hunts last digits a rule can never reach, or grows a shared-side matchstick row to explain 3n + 1.

lab_teaches.evidence: Six steps: make 8 terms of 'add 3' from 1 by picking the next term (wrong ×3 and +1 options explained), label each term odd or even and see the switch, test +2, +3, +4, +5 from 1 with dot pairs and the red odd-one-out dot, tap the five last digits 'add 4' from 2 never reaches, grow matchstick squares and choose the count for 10, then the challenge. The learner discovers each feature before the banner states the reason.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options the lab disproves: whether 100 is a term of 'add 3' from 1 (many say no because 100 is not in the 3 times table; the banner shows 99 = 33 jumps), whether the odd/even switch breaks somewhere or only holds for small numbers, and whether 'add 4' from 2 can ever end in 5 if you go far enough. The reveal repeats the learner's own choice.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions (4th term of 'add 5' from 2, features of 'add 2' from 1, is 50 a term of 'add 3', sticks for 6 squares, last digit of 'add 10' from 3, why 'add 3' switches) with answer order rotated. Twelve distinct wrong-answer messages name the slip: extra jump, multiplying instead of adding, only odd steps switch, judging from the first term, passing a number is not hitting it, parity is not enough, shared sides counted twice, missing the first stick, adding 10 keeps the ones digit, size and start are not the reason.

readability.evidence: validate_lessons readability passed (kid text well under 6.5, adult under 9.5 by learn/readability.py). Kid paragraphs use short sentences and concrete pictures (dots in pairs, sticks, last digits); the terms term, rule, odd, even and last digit are explained where first used. Lab banners are one or two short sentences and wrap inside the canvas at 360 px.

no_filler.evidence: No filler patterns matched (gate_content). Every kid paragraph does one job: make terms from a rule, spot and explain the odd/even switch, contrast even steps and last-digit cycles, then the matchstick shape rule. Adult text gives the standards, what each lab step shows, the checked figures and the named common mistakes, with no repeated template sentences.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 × 640 (2x) in light and dark themes for all six steps: term boxes wrap to two rows of 4 (8 terms) or 5 (10 terms), odd/even tags sit inside the boxes after the overlap seen in the first sheet was fixed, the matchstick squares were redrawn after the first sheet showed slanted sides, header boxes grow to fit wrapped text, and chips are at least 42 px tall. Nothing is clipped.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas tap has a button twin in the lab button group (next-term choices, Odd/Even, Add 2–5, Ends in 0–9, + square and the stick answers). The canvas aria-label is rewritten after every action with the terms, labels, rules tested or stick count. The browser gate ran axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) on desktop and iPhone 13 in both themes with no violations and no console errors; the wrong-path click sweep raised no errors.
